name: Hana Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, that's fine. I'm Hana, I'm 27, and I'm in my second year as an apprentice lineworker with a rural electric co-op. I live with my partner Jonas, who's a night-shift nurse, in a rented flat above a bakery in the valley.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Then let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the depot by 6:30, coffee in the cab, and our foreman Pete Novak hands out the job packets. Most days I'm the ground hand: digging, hauling, rigging, passing tools up to whoever's in the bucket, and climbing when Pete lets me practise. The lights coming back on in somebody's kitchen at three in the morning is the best feeling I know. A robot won't feel that. What wears me out is standby week, when the phone can go any hour and the cold gets into your hands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned climbing practice. Where are you with that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, I'm behind. The two lads who started with me are quicker up a pole, and I'm still nervous on the gaff, the spike on your climbing boot. My test is in the spring, and I study for the written part with a chatbot now and then, quizzing me on grounding rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Okay, that's basically what Pete says every time someone mentions AI in the break room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what most of us already say: it's a fancy autocomplete. Nobody's going to fix a snapped pole in a blizzard with a chatbot. The worst part of my week would still be the frozen fingers, not the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be a relief. My job is hands-on, the co-op isn't going anywhere, and the union contract gives me a pay step every six months. My real worries would be my climbing test and our rent, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and pass the pole-climbing assessment by spring. I'd keep putting about 300 a month into savings for a house deposit, which is roughly four months of bills right now. And I'd keep using the chatbot for flashcards, because it's cheaper than the prep book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit boring, maybe, but boring is good when you're two years into a four-year apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says AI automates some routine tasks. Which bits of your day would that touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork, mainly. We fill in timesheets and job notes on a tablet, and half the time it eats them. If AI just filled those in from photos, Pete would stop shouting at me on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leaving AI aside, is there anything that's already weighing on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent went up eight percent in September, and the landlord already hinted at more. Jonas works nights, so we barely see each other, and we keep saying we'll buy somewhere in two years. That's the thing I lie awake about, not AI.

say: AI is a **fancy autocomplete**, and a **snapped pole** in a blizzard still needs a person.
The hard part of this job is the **cold and the hours**, not the computers.
think: I feel **relieved**, because my work is hands-on and the **co-op** is steady.
My real worries are the **climbing test** and the **rent rise**, not machines.
do: Pass the **pole-climbing assessment** by spring and keep practising on the training pole after shifts.
Save about **300 a month** toward a house deposit with my partner Jonas.
Keep using a chatbot for **exam flashcards** because it's cheaper than the prep book.
feel: **Calm** and a little bored, which feels fine two years into an **apprenticeship**.
S0.quote: Nobody's going to fix a snapped pole in a blizzard with a chatbot. The worst part of my week would still be the frozen fingers, not the computers.
fieldNote: Her **security** rests on the union contract and the fact that her work is **hands-on**.
She admitted she is **behind at climbing** before I asked, which is honest for a junior.
The pressures she names are **rent** and her **test**, both unrelated to AI.

steps.text: Pass the pole-climbing assessment by spring
Put 300 a month into a house deposit fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one sounds more like what's actually happening, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the power still gets fixed by hand, and anyone who thinks a laptop can climb a pole hasn't met one. Online I'd probably share the union's posts about protecting office jobs. I'm not loud online, but I'd share those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my bit is safe for a long while. The thinking side of the co-op would change though: dispatch, the storeroom ordering, the people planning our jobs. I'd lose friends in the office long before I lost anything myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our shop steward Gary to put me on the union's technology committee, to push for no layoffs, only retraining, in the office. I'd try the new outage app once the senior guys say it's not rubbish. And I'd keep saving, same as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much as for the people who'd go quietly while we're all out on the trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the co-op would you worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Rosa answers angry billing calls all day. A chatbot could take that job by Christmas, and nobody is going to teach Rosa to climb poles. And Doug, the estimator who prices our jobs, is 61 and hates computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say your own job is safe, but you'd still get involved. Why bother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it starts with them and works its way down. If nobody in the union says anything when the call centre shrinks, nobody will listen when it's the trucks. My dad lost his factory job like that, one department at a time.

say: The power still gets fixed **by hand**, and a laptop can't **climb** a pole.
I'd share the union's posts about **protecting office jobs** at the co-op.
think: My own **hands-on work** is safe for a long while yet.
**Dispatch**, ordering and billing would shrink, and I'd lose **office friends** first.
If nobody defends the office now, nobody will defend the **trucks** later.
do: Ask the shop steward Gary for a seat on the union's **technology committee**.
Push for **retraining instead of layoffs** for billing and dispatch staff.
Try the new **outage app** once senior lineworkers say it works.
feel: **Uneasy** for colleagues like Rosa, more than **worried** for herself.
S1.quote: My friend Rosa answers angry billing calls all day. A chatbot could take that job by Christmas, and nobody is going to teach Rosa to climb poles.
fieldNote: She sees the change landing on **office staff** first and feels loyalty to them.
Her father's **factory job loss** shapes her belief that cuts move department by department.
Typical of a **steady** adopter: she'll use the app only after **senior crew** approve it.

steps.text: Join the union technology committee through shop steward Gary
Try the outage app once senior crew say it works
Keep up the pole training and the 300 a month savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's when I'd be finishing my apprenticeship, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say what the union says: slow it down, and keep a qualified person on every live line. I'd go to the rallies if there were rallies. I'd be angry online, probably for the first time in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship in 2028 and get maybe three years at full journeyman pay. Then a robot takes the bucket truck, and I'm 32 and starting over. Journeyman means fully qualified, and that's the whole reason I took the low apprentice pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop eating out and push savings from 300 to 600 a month. I'd go to every union meeting and write to our local representative about a training fund paid for by the companies making the robots. And Jonas and I would stop house hunting, because a mortgage on my wage would be madness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like when you're on the ground and you hear a crossarm crack above you, and there's a second where you don't know which way it's falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says the thinking work goes first and robots come about three years later. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side of the co-op goes in 2028, so the planning and dispatch would be done by AI the day I qualify. Then I'd have about three years where it's just us and the trucks, taking orders from a computer. Those three years are when I'd have to save every penny and find a way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas the night you realised this was real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jonas that the hospital is safer than the poles now, and that he might have to carry us for a while. That would be hard to say. I've always been proud of paying my half.

say: We need to **slow it down** and keep a qualified person on every live line.
I'd turn up at **union rallies** and be openly angry online for once.
think: I'd qualify in **2028** and get only about **three years** at full pay.
By **2031** a robot takes the bucket truck, and I'm **starting over** at 32.
do: Double savings to **600 a month** by cutting eating out and takeaways.
Write to our local representative about a **training fund** paid by robot makers.
Stop **house hunting** with Jonas until the picture is clearer.
feel: **Sick**, like hearing a **crossarm crack** overhead and not knowing where it falls.
Hurt **pride** at the thought of Jonas carrying the household.
S2.quote: I'd finish my apprenticeship in 2028 and get maybe three years at full journeyman pay. Then a robot takes the bucket truck, and I'm 32 and starting over.
fieldNote: The **timing** hits her hardest: AGI lands exactly as she **qualifies**.
She treats the **three-year gap** as a window to save, not as safety.
Her partner's **nursing job** is the household's backstop, and admitting that cost her something.

steps.text: Raise monthly savings from 300 to 600 by cutting takeaways
Attend every union meeting and rally about live-line staffing
Write to the local representative about a robot-funded training fund
Pause house hunting with Jonas until the jobs picture settles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So I'd qualify, get a few years in, and then it comes. That's different from the last one, but not as different as I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this properly, so let's make the companies plan for it with us, not around us. At the depot I'd be the one nagging people to come to meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years of warning is enough to get scared but not enough to change trades twice. I'd get journeyman pay from 2028, so I'd have money for once. But robots in 2034 would still catch me at 35, right in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship and then sign up for the co-op's evening course on maintaining the new automated equipment, if they ran one. I'd keep saving 500 a month, and push the union to get the course paid and in work hours. I'd also keep going on the committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a steadier kind. More like the week before a test than standing under a falling crossarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those extra years let you do that the two-year version doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years at full pay, mainly, so a proper cushion, maybe eight months instead of four. And time to see which robots actually work in mud and ice. I'm not jumping at the first shiny thing; I'd want to see it on a real crew first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would you pick: stay on the trucks or go for the tech course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the tech course, but only once I'd seen someone on our crew do it and come out with a decent job. I'm not first through the door. I'm second, once someone shows it's safe.

say: We have time, so the companies should **plan with us**, not around us.
I'd nag everyone at the depot to come to **union meetings**.
think: **Full pay from 2028** would finally give me a proper cushion.
Robots in **2034** would still catch me at **35**, mid-career.
Five years is long enough to worry but short for a **second trade**.
do: Finish the **apprenticeship** and then join an evening course on **automated equipment** upkeep.
Save **500 a month** to build about eight months of cushion.
Push the union to get the course **paid** and in work hours.
feel: **Anxious** in a steadier way, like the week before a **test**.
S3.quote: Five years of warning is enough to get scared but not enough to change trades twice.
fieldNote: The extra years mean **full pay** first, which she sees as her main protection.
She describes herself as **second through the door** and waits for proof from her crew.
Her plan depends on the **co-op offering** a course, which she can't control.

steps.text: Join the co-op evening course on automated line equipment
Save 500 a month toward eight months of cushion
Push the union to make the course paid and in work hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, now I can breathe a bit. I'd be 37 when the thinking side goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to retrain everyone who needs it, so there's no excuse to leave anyone behind. I'd push that line at work and at the union picnic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I can be the person who signs off the robot's work instead of the person it replaces. I'd be a senior lineworker by then, maybe a trainer. Someone has to check the robot did the grounding right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, then around 2030 start a part-time two-year electrical technology diploma at the college in town. I'd keep saving 400 a month and keep going on the committee. Otherwise I'd carry on climbing poles and enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It's like hearing a storm is coming next week, not tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd be starting over at 32. What's different at 40?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 40 I'd have twelve years of experience and a diploma. I'd be the person who knows what a line should look like when the robot's done. At 32 I'd have been the newest one out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Jonas buy that house in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, but a small one, and only with a fixed rate. Jonas's job looks safe, and mine would have a decade of pay in it. I'd still want six months saved before we signed anything.

say: A **decade** is time to retrain everyone, so there's **no excuse** for leaving people behind.
I'd make that point at work and at the **union picnic**.
think: I could become the person who **signs off** robot work, not the one replaced.
By **2036** I'd be a senior lineworker, maybe a **trainer**.
do: Start a part-time **electrical technology diploma** at the town college around **2030**.
Keep saving **400 a month** and stay on the union committee.
Buy a **small house** with Jonas on a fixed rate after six months' savings.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to breathe, like a storm forecast for **next week**.
S4.quote: With ten years, I can be the person who signs off the robot's work instead of the person it replaces.
fieldNote: Ten years flips her from **newest** out the door to an experienced **checker** of robot work.
She still wants a **diploma** as insurance rather than trusting seniority alone.
The house plan returns, but **small and fixed-rate**, showing her caution.

steps.text: Carry on climbing and finish the apprenticeship
Start a part-time electrical technology diploma around 2030
Keep saving 400 a month before signing any mortgage
Buy a small house with Jonas on a fixed rate

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. It lands the year I qualify, and robots come before I've built anything up. What would help is retraining that's paid, in work hours, and won by the union, plus a rule that a qualified person stays on every live line for safety.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about being a woman on the crew. I'm the only one, and I'm the lowest on the seniority list. If there are cuts, I'm first out, and I'd want someone to notice who keeps getting pushed out first.

headlineQuote: The lights coming back on in somebody's kitchen at three in the morning is the best feeling I know. A robot won't feel that.
portrait: Hana is a 27-year-old **second-year apprentice** at a rural electric **co-op**, living with her nurse partner Jonas.
She is behind on **climbing**, honest about it, and loves the moment **power** comes back on.
A firm **union** believer, she sees cuts starting with **office staff** and moving down to the trucks.
Her fear peaks with **AGI by 2028**, which arrives exactly as she **qualifies**.
With ten years she plans a **diploma** and a role **checking robot work**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive about three years after she qualifies.
As the only woman and lowest on **seniority**, she expects to be **first cut**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** in work hours, won by the union.
A rule keeping a **qualified person** on every **live line**.
